title: 'Most of my pension has gone on home heating oil'
content: Pensioners across Northern Ireland are facing an increasingly difficult choice between heating their homes and meeting other essential expenses as heating oil prices continue to climb. The situation has become particularly acute in the region, where many households rely on oil-fired heating systems rather than mains gas. For many on fixed incomes, the rising cost of heating oil represents a significant and growing burden on already stretched budgets. One pensioner's stark statement that most of their pension has gone towards home heating oil illustrates the real hardship being experienced across Northern Ireland. As winter months approach, families are forced to make difficult decisions about how to allocate limited resources. The problem is especially pronounced in Northern Ireland compared to other parts of the UK. Many rural and semi-rural areas across the province depend on oil heating, making residents particularly vulnerable to price fluctuations in the global oil market. Unlike those connected to mains gas networks, households using oil heating have fewer alternatives and cannot easily switch suppliers or fuel types. Several factors have contributed to the current crisis. International oil prices have remained elevated, and transportation costs to Northern Ireland add an additional premium to heating oil prices. Supply chain disruptions and ongoing global economic pressures continue to keep costs high for consumers. The impact extends beyond pensioners, affecting families with young children and those with disabilities who require consistent heating for health reasons. Community organisations and charities across Northern Ireland have reported increased demand for support and advice from households struggling with fuel poverty. Local politicians and energy campaigners have called for greater support for affected households. Discussions continue about potential assistance schemes and whether additional help should be targeted at those most vulnerable to fuel poverty. As temperatures drop in the coming months, the situation is expected to intensify. Many households are already rationing their heating use, keeping homes at lower temperatures than recommended for health and wellbeing. The long-term sustainability of this situation remains a serious concern for policymakers and community leaders across Northern Ireland.
summary: Rising heating oil prices are hitting Northern Ireland harder than the rest of the UK - here's everything you need to know.
author: BBC News

title: Oil price jumps after Qatar warns all Gulf production could stop within days
content: Oil prices have surged following stark warnings from Qatar's Energy Minister Saad al-Kaabi that Gulf states could halt energy exports within days if the escalating conflict involving Iran persists. In an interview with the Financial Times, al-Kaabi revealed that Qatar has already suspended liquefied natural gas production after an Iranian drone strike hit its key Ras Laffan facility. This plant handles a significant share of global LNG supply, vital for markets in Asia and Europe. He predicted that other Gulf producers would soon follow suit, declaring force majeure—legal clauses excusing contract breaches due to unforeseen events like war. The minister cautioned that continued hostilities could block the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial chokepoint for much of the world's oil shipments. If tankers cannot pass safely, crude prices might rocket to $150 a barrel within weeks, he said. Even if fighting stops immediately, restarting normal exports could take weeks to months due to damage assessments and logistical hurdles. Markets reacted swiftly. By midday in Europe, West Texas Intermediate crude climbed over 6% to more than $86 a barrel, while Brent crude rose above $89, up more than 4%. The volatility stems from fears of broader disruptions, including an attack that shut down a US-operated oil field in Iraq's Kurdistan region. Explosions near Erbil airport and drone strikes have heightened tensions, drawing the area deeper into the regional conflict. Al-Kaabi painted a grim picture for the global economy. Prolonged shutdowns would spike energy costs worldwide, trigger product shortages, and force factories to idle, potentially derailing GDP growth everywhere. "This will bring down the economies of the world," he warned, urging an end to hostilities for any chance of recovery. US President Donald Trump has pledged naval escorts for vessels through the strait, but al-Kaabi dismissed the idea as too risky amid ongoing attacks. Qatar insists it will resume output only after a full ceasefire. The crisis underscores the fragility of global energy supplies amid Middle East strife. Gulf nations, home to some of the largest reserves, now face unprecedented threats, rippling through fuel prices, inflation, and supply chains far beyond the region. As diplomats scramble for de-escalation, traders brace for more turbulence.
summary: Energy Minister Saad al-Kaabi says oil could hit $150 a barrel if the Iran conflict continues over the coming weeks.
author: BBC News

title: Council considers extending food voucher scheme
content: A local council is poised to extend its popular food voucher scheme, offering vital support to families facing hardship during school holidays. The initiative targets households eligible for free school meals, providing supermarket vouchers to help cover essential grocery costs when children are not at school. This move comes as part of a broader Crisis and Resilience Fund, with the council allocating significant resources to sustain the programme. Officials have earmarked substantial funding to ensure vouchers reach those in need, reflecting ongoing concerns about the cost of living pressures affecting communities across the region. The scheme has already proven a lifeline for many families, bridging the gap left by the absence of school-provided meals over holidays. Parents have welcomed the support, which allows them to purchase fresh food and basics without dipping further into strained budgets. One local resident described it as "a real game-changer," enabling better meal planning during tough times. Council leaders emphasise the importance of this extension amid rising inflation and energy costs. The fund draws inspiration from national efforts, including the government's Household Support Fund, which has been prolonged to cover the coming year. This alignment underscores a coordinated approach to tackling poverty at both local and national levels. Discussions at the council meeting highlighted the scheme's success since its inception. Data shows increased uptake during previous holidays, with vouchers redeemed widely at major supermarkets. Extending it would secure continuity, potentially benefiting thousands of children and their families. Critics, however, question the long-term sustainability of such targeted aid. Some councillors argue for wider reforms, like universal free school meals, to address root causes. Yet proponents counter that immediate relief is crucial while broader solutions are developed. The decision is expected soon, with approval likely to bring swift relief ahead of upcoming breaks. This reflects the council's commitment to resilience in the face of economic challenges, ensuring no family goes hungry due to circumstance. Community groups have praised the proactive stance, urging swift implementation. As debates continue, the focus remains on delivering tangible help where it's needed most, fostering a stronger, more supportive local network.
summary: The council earmarks £1m to pay for the vouchers as part of a new Crisis and Resilience Fund.

title: US economy unexpectedly sheds 92,000 jobs in February
content: The US economy delivered a stark shock in February as payrolls plummeted far below expectations, marking a significant downturn in the labour market. Economists had anticipated modest job gains, but official figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics revealed a sharp contraction across nearly every sector, with private payrolls bearing the brunt of the losses. This unexpected weakness follows downward revisions to prior months' data, painting a picture of a cooling jobs market that has persisted for much of the year. The unemployment rate edged higher to 4.4 per cent, reflecting broader challenges as employment figures in key industries faltered. Health care, typically a reliable source of growth, saw substantial setbacks partly due to temporary strikes at major providers like Kaiser Permanente, which disrupted survey periods. Other sectors echoed the gloom, with notable declines in manufacturing, information services, construction, transportation, leisure and hospitality, and educational services. Federal government employment continued its steep slide, exacerbating concerns over public sector cuts that have rippled through vital services. Gains were limited, appearing in areas like social assistance and certain state government roles, but they offered little offset to the overall bleed. Wage growth provided a sliver of positivity, ticking up slightly year-over-year and outpacing inflation for an extended period, a sign often linked to rising productivity. Yet this comes amid mounting pressures from elevated oil prices, complicating the Federal Reserve's delicate balancing act between curbing inflation and supporting employment. Analysts warn that the softening labour market could signal deeper economic headwinds, especially as three-month job growth averages have dwindled alarmingly low. Private sector losses dominated, with temporary factors like strikes accounting for a notable portion, though underlying trends point to structural strains in manufacturing and federal roles since early last year. The report has ignited debate over policy responses, with the Fed facing tough choices as slower hiring collides with persistent inflationary risks. For American workers and businesses, February's figures underscore a precarious moment, raising questions about the sustainability of recent economic resilience in the face of these sectoral slumps.
summary: The contraction came as a surprise with payrolls down in nearly every sector.
author: BBC News

title: Large portions and good value - Warrington chippy expert gives his latest verdict
content: A Warrington chippy connoisseur has delivered glowing praise for a Widnes takeaway, highlighting its generous portions and unbeatable value in the latest stop on a nationwide quest to champion Britain's best fish-and-chip shops. The Chippy Tour, a popular venture crisscrossing the UK, aims to spotlight traditional chippies that keep the classic British supper alive. Led by a Warrington-based expert with a keen palate for the perfect batter and chips, the tour has been visiting eateries far and wide, rating them on taste, freshness, and that all-important portion size. This time, the spotlight fell on The Widnes Fryer, a local favourite in the heart of Widnes. The expert was impressed by the shop's commitment to quality, noting how it serves up hefty helpings of golden haddock in crisp batter, alongside thick-cut chips that avoid the soggy pitfall so many places fall into. "Large portions and good value" summed up the verdict, with the meal ticking all the boxes for a satisfying, no-frills feed. Fish and chips remain a cornerstone of British cuisine, with chippies like this one embodying community spirit. The Widnes Fryer, a staple for locals, sources fresh fish daily and fries everything to order, steering clear of the mass-produced alternatives creeping into the high street. The tour's organiser praised the shop's old-school charm, from the sizzling vats to the friendly banter at the counter. Warrington and Widnes, just a stone's throw apart across the Mersey, share a proud tradition of top-notch takeaways. This endorsement comes at a time when independent chippies face rising costs from energy bills and ingredients, yet places like The Widnes Fryer soldier on, offering meals that punch above their price weight. The Chippy Tour has already racked up visits to coastal spots and inland gems, building a loyal following among foodies who crave authenticity over gimmicks. Fans are encouraged to nominate their own favourites, keeping the spotlight on unsung heroes of the British plate. For those in Cheshire, this latest review is a call to action: head to Widnes for a plate that delivers on promise. As the tour rolls on, it reminds us why fish and chips isn't just food—it's a national treasure, one crispy bite at a time.
summary: THE Chippy Tour is a nationwide journey celebrating traditional fish-and-chip shops across the UK.
author: Warrington Guardian

title: Councillor reveals ongoing four-year hate campaign waged against her
content: A local councillor has spoken out about a sustained harassment campaign that has targeted her for four years, revealing the toll that online abuse has taken on her personal and professional life. The councillor disclosed that she has been subjected to hundreds of messages across social media platforms as part of what she describes as a coordinated hate campaign. The relentless nature of the abuse has prompted her to come forward publicly, hoping to raise awareness about the challenges faced by elected representatives in the digital age. Online harassment of public figures has become an increasingly serious issue across the UK. Councillors and other elected officials often find themselves on the receiving end of abusive messages, threats, and coordinated campaigns that can have significant mental health impacts. The anonymity provided by social media platforms can embolden individuals to send messages they might never deliver face to face. The councillor's decision to speak openly about her experience reflects a growing movement among public servants to address the problem directly. By naming the issue and discussing its impact, she hopes to encourage both the public and social media companies to take the matter more seriously. The campaign against her appears to have escalated over the four-year period, with the volume and intensity of messages creating a distressing environment. Such sustained attacks can affect not only the targeted individual but also their family members and colleagues who witness the abuse. Social media platforms have faced mounting criticism for their handling of harassment and hate speech. While many have implemented reporting mechanisms and community guidelines, critics argue that enforcement remains inconsistent and often inadequate, particularly when targeting public figures. The councillor's willingness to speak publicly about her experience may help shine a light on a problem that many elected representatives face in silence. Her case serves as a reminder of the human cost of online abuse and the importance of fostering respectful discourse, particularly in local politics where representatives are often accessible members of their own communities.
summary: "A campaign of hundreds of messages started on social media"
author: Cheshire Live

title: Chester family dog needed life-saving op after swallowing fruit stone
content: A Chester family faced a frightening ordeal when their beloved dog suddenly fell unwell after swallowing a fruit stone, requiring urgent life-saving surgery to save her life. The incident unfolded in the historic city of Chester, where the family noticed their pet becoming lethargic and distressed. What began as a typical day turned into panic as symptoms worsened, prompting a swift rush to the veterinary clinic. Vets quickly diagnosed the problem: the stone had lodged in her digestive system, posing a severe risk of blockage or perforation. In a race against time, the dog underwent emergency surgery. The procedure, described as delicate and complex, successfully removed the obstruction, allowing her a fighting chance at recovery. The family expressed immense relief, crediting the veterinary team's rapid response with preventing a tragic outcome. Such mishaps highlight the hidden dangers pets face from everyday household items. Fruit stones, often overlooked amid kitchen scraps or garden play, can prove deadly for curious dogs. Experts warn that items like peach, apricot, or cherry pits contain not only hard cores that cause choking or intestinal blockages but also cyanogenic compounds, which release toxins when chewed. This case echoes similar stories across Cheshire, where pet owners have learned harsh lessons about vigilance. Local vets report a rise in such emergencies, especially during summer when fresh produce abounds. "Dogs explore the world with their mouths," one area veterinarian noted, urging families to secure bins and supervise playtime. Recovery has been steady for the Chester dog, who is now back home, wagging her tail and regaining strength. The family has since childproofed their home further, disposing of fruit waste securely and sharing their story to raise awareness. Incidents like this underscore the vital role of pet insurance and prompt medical care in the UK, where veterinary costs can soar into thousands for emergency ops. Cheshire's animal lovers are reminded to stay alert— a small stone can lead to big troubles, but quick action makes all the difference. The family now cherishes every moment with their furry companion, vowing to prevent any repeat scares. Their experience serves as a timely reminder for all dog owners in the region to prioritise safety amid the joys of pet parenthood.
summary: She became unwell

title: Chester Zoo's safari-style lodge resort opens to public for lunch and afternoon tea
content: Chester Zoo has thrown open the doors of its luxurious safari-style lodge resort to day visitors, allowing everyone to savour lunch and afternoon tea without needing an overnight booking. The Reserve, a collection of 51 high-end lodges nestled alongside the zoo's Heart of Africa savannah, first welcomed overnight guests in August 2025. Picture giraffes and zebras wandering just beyond your table, or a serene lakeside setting for a relaxing bite. This move makes the resort's dining spots, like the Tsavo Lounge and Amboseli Restaurant, accessible to a wider crowd. Families, couples and friends can now drop in for hearty lunches or indulgent afternoon teas, complete with firepit sundowners on balmy evenings. It's a clever way to let more people taste the magic of glamping vibes without committing to a full stay. Chester Zoo bosses say every booking and visit helps fund their conservation efforts, protecting species across Africa and the UK. The lodges offer savannah-facing balconies where antelope roam freely, and peaceful options by the water. Day trippers get a slice of that immersion, perhaps spotting animals up close while tucking into fresh dishes. The timing couldn't be better, with a special Mother's Day afternoon tea on the cards to draw in crowds. It's part of Cheshire's booming lineup of must-do experiences in 2026, blending wildlife wonders with gourmet treats. Whether you're after behind-the-scenes tours or just a posh cream tea, The Reserve delivers. Local foodies are buzzing about the on-site bar and restaurant, praising the family-friendly setup with hot tubs and terraces nearby. No longer just for those splashing out on a lodge night, it's an inviting add-on to a zoo day out. This opening taps into the growing demand for unique dining with a view, putting Chester Zoo firmly on the map as a top spot for wildlife lovers and lunch seekers alike. Expect queues as word spreads – it's the perfect excuse to blend animal spotting with a spot of luxury.
summary: You now don't have to be staying in one of the lodges to visit

title: Axel Springer agrees to buy Telegraph Media Group in £575m deal
content: German media giant Axel Springer has agreed to acquire the Telegraph Media Group for £575 million in cash, marking a significant development in the ownership of one of Britain's most prominent news organisations. The deal represents a major investment in the historic Fleet Street title and comes after a period of uncertainty for the company and its staff. The agreement between Axel Springer and RedBird IMI, the current owner, aims to preserve the integrity of the Telegraph brand whilst providing it with a platform for growth and expansion. Both parties have emphasised their commitment to maintaining high-quality, independent journalism and media plurality in the UK. The transaction is expected to be discussed with the Department of Culture, Media and Sports and other stakeholders in the coming weeks as part of the regulatory approval process. Axel Springer, a transatlantic family-owned media company, has outlined ambitious plans for the Telegraph's future. The publisher intends to turbocharge the newspaper's expansion into the United States market, leveraging expertise from its existing media brands including POLITICO and BUSINESS INSIDER. The Telegraph will also gain access to Axel Springer's proven track record in developing digital journalism and artificial intelligence applications, alongside commercial expertise in digital advertising, subscriptions and events. RedBird IMI has expressed satisfaction with the agreement, noting that Axel Springer's strong commercial offer and straightforward regulatory path to ownership position the publisher well to take the Telegraph forward. The deal comes at a time when the newspaper's journalists and employees have endured an extended period of uncertainty regarding the company's future. This acquisition represents a notable moment for British media, bringing a major international publisher into ownership of a heritage title with a significant readership and influence. The Telegraph has long been a cornerstone of British journalism, and the new ownership structure is expected to provide the resources and strategic direction needed to navigate the evolving media landscape and compete effectively in both domestic and international markets.
summary: Last year the Daily Mail and General Trust proposed to buy the company in a £500m takeover.
author: BBC News

title: German media giant to buy Telegraph in £575m deal
content: A German media powerhouse, Axel Springer, has struck a deal to acquire the Telegraph Media Group for £575 million, marking a significant shift in the ownership of one of Britain's most iconic newspapers. The agreement, announced by Axel Springer, sees the company buying out RedBird IMI's stake in the Daily Telegraph, Sunday Telegraph, and their digital operations. This cash transaction ends months of uncertainty surrounding the future of the titles, which had been caught up in regulatory scrutiny over previous foreign ownership bids. Axel Springer, a family-owned firm with a strong transatlantic presence, described the move as a way to safeguard the Telegraph's heritage while propelling it into new markets. Company leaders highlighted plans to expand the newspaper's reach into the United States, drawing on expertise from their own brands like POLITICO and Business Insider. They also promised to share know-how in digital journalism, artificial intelligence, subscriptions, and advertising to bolster the Telegraph's commercial edge. Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer CEO, emphasised the human side of the deal, acknowledging the prolonged uncertainty faced by Telegraph journalists and staff. "We want to bring that uncertainty to an end as soon as we can and welcome you into Axel Springer," he said, underscoring a commitment to high-quality, independent reporting. RedBird IMI, the seller, praised the swift negotiations and Axel Springer's robust commercial proposal. They expressed confidence in a straightforward path through UK regulatory approvals, noting close collaboration with the government to finalise the sale. The deal is expected to come under review by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, amid ongoing debates about media plurality and foreign influence in British journalism. This acquisition brings a fresh dynamic to Fleet Street, introducing a German giant known for its conservative-leaning titles like Bild and Die Welt. For the Telegraph, long a stalwart of right-of-centre commentary, it signals potential for global growth but also raises questions about editorial independence under overseas ownership. Both parties stressed the benefits for readers, employees, and the UK media landscape, positioning the takeover as a vote of confidence in quality journalism amid digital disruption. As discussions with regulators progress, the focus will turn to how Axel Springer's resources can revitalise the Telegraph in an increasingly competitive market.
summary: German media giant Axel Springer is to buy Telegraph Media Group in a £575m deal that will see the Daily and Sunday Telegraph print titles and their online business come under overseas ownership.

title: Price of first class stamps to rise to £1.80
content: The price of a first class stamp is set to increase to £1.80, Royal Mail has announced, marking another significant hike for everyday postal users. The postal service explained that the rise, effective from later this year, is necessary to offset soaring delivery costs. Factors include higher wages for staff, increased fuel prices, and the ongoing shift away from letter volumes as more people turn to digital communication. Royal Mail emphasised that these pressures have been building for years, with the universal service obligation requiring them to deliver mail to every UK address six days a week. This will be the latest in a series of increases, following rises that have seen first class stamps jump from 95p in 2022 to £1.35 last year. Second class stamps will also go up, to around £1.05, though exact details are still being finalised. Businesses and households reliant on post for bills, statements, and parcels will feel the pinch, especially amid the cost-of-living squeeze. Consumer groups have reacted with fury, branding the move as "punitive" for loyal customers. Which?, the influential consumer champion, warned that frequent price jumps risk pricing people out of using the post entirely. "Royal Mail is caught in a vicious cycle of declining volumes and rising costs, but passing it all onto consumers without alternatives feels unfair," a spokesperson said. They called for government intervention to reform the universal service, arguing that the current model is unsustainable in a digital age. Campaigners like Citizens Advice echoed these concerns, highlighting how vulnerable groups—such as the elderly or those without smartphones—depend on physical mail. "This isn't just about stamps; it's about access to essential services," they noted. Some are urging Ofcom, the regulator, to scrutinise the plans closely and explore incentives for efficiency. Royal Mail, however, insists the changes are vital for long-term survival. The company has faced strikes, network strains from parcels during the pandemic boom, and competition from private couriers. Without such adjustments, they argue, service quality could suffer. Public reaction online has been swift, with many venting frustration over what feels like relentless inflation on a basic necessity. As the nation grapples with broader economic woes, this stamp hike serves as a stark reminder of how even small costs are climbing. Regulators now face pressure to balance Royal Mail's needs with protecting everyday users.
summary: Royal Mail says the increase reflects the rise in delivery costs, but the move angers consumer groups.
author: BBC News

title: Xbox confirms new console is coming - but can it revive the brand?
content: Microsoft has officially unveiled plans for its next-generation Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, marking a bold move to reinvigorate the brand amid shifting industry dynamics. Asha Sharma, the newly appointed CEO of Microsoft Gaming, shared the exciting announcement on social media earlier this week. Taking over following Phil Spencer's retirement after nearly four decades with the company, Sharma wasted no time in signalling her vision for Xbox's future. "Great start to the morning with Team Xbox, where we talked about our commitment to the return of Xbox, including Project Helix, the code name for our next generation console," she wrote. Project Helix promises to lead in performance and crucially, play both Xbox and PC games, confirming long-rumoured hybrid capabilities. This development comes at a critical juncture for Microsoft. Xbox has faced challenges in recent years, with major franchises like those from its studios increasingly appearing on rival platforms such as PlayStation. The strategy of fewer exclusives has diluted the appeal of Xbox hardware, prompting questions about its place in a market dominated by Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo. Sharma's tease emphasises a "return" to Xbox roots, potentially blending high-end console power with the flexibility of PC gaming to attract a broader audience. Details remain scarce, with no specifics on specs, pricing or release date revealed yet. However, Sharma has promised more insights at the Game Developers Conference next week, where she will engage with partners and studios. A accompanying video showcased the Project Helix logo and a possible startup sound, fuelling speculation about its premium design. Reports suggest collaboration with AMD, positioning it as a "tailored experience" in line with previous teases from former Xbox president Sarah Bond. The hybrid nature of Project Helix could reshape competition. By supporting PC titles, it directly challenges high-end PCs and even emerging devices like Valve's Steam Machine. Yet, industry hurdles loom, including global memory shortages that have delayed other hardware launches. Fans are buzzing online, with calls for revived projects like Scalebound amid uncertainty over Xbox's direction. For Microsoft, success hinges on whether Project Helix can convince gamers to invest in new hardware. With Xbox's ecosystem expanding across cloud, PC and now this versatile console, Sharma's leadership will be tested. As the gaming world awaits GDC revelations, one thing is clear: Microsoft is doubling down on hardware to reclaim its console throne.
summary: Microsoft is the first big company out of the gates with Project Helix - a "next-generation" console.
author: BBC News

title: This is when people in Cheshire can see a Spitfire pass
content: Residents of Cheshire are in for a treat as a historic Spitfire, Britain's most iconic aircraft from the Second World War, prepares to soar overhead in a special flypast. The event forms part of nationwide celebrations marking the 90th anniversary of the Royal Air Force, offering a poignant reminder of the plane's legendary role in defending the skies. The Spitfire, with its elegant elliptical wings and unmistakable roar, became a symbol of defiance during the Battle of Britain in 1940. Pilots like the highly decorated Leonard Cheshire, Cheshire's own war hero, flew similar aircraft and bombers in daring missions that turned the tide of the conflict. Cheshire, the youngest group captain in the RAF, led operations from bases near the county, including RAF Linton-on-Ouse in Yorkshire, where he commanded squadrons flying Halifax bombers. His bravery, such as returning damaged over Cologne to complete a bomb run on a marshalling yard, earned him the Distinguished Service Order and cemented his place in aviation history. This flypast will trace a path over key areas including North Mid Wales and Chester, thrilling aviation enthusiasts and families alike. Organised by the RAF, it celebrates not just the Spitfire's engineering marvel but the courage of those who flew it. The aircraft, preserved in flying condition, represents a bygone era when these fighters outmanoeuvred Luftwaffe foes, protecting British cities from invasion. Local excitement is building, with spotters advised to look skyward at the specified time for the low-level pass. Such events are rare opportunities to witness living history, evoking memories of wartime resilience. In Cheshire, where airfields like those at Marston Moor once buzzed with activity under leaders like Cheshire, the sight will stir pride and reflection. The anniversary underscores the RAF's enduring legacy, from precision bombing techniques honed in the 1940s to modern air power. Communities are encouraged to gather safely outdoors, cameras at the ready, to honour the past while inspiring the next generation. As the Merlin engine echoes across the landscape, it serves as a timeless tribute to innovation and valour that helped secure victory.
summary: THE Spitfire, the most famous plane in British history, will fly over Cheshire as part of 90th anniversary celebrations.
author: Warrington Guardian

title: School celebrates World Book Day with a creative orange theme
content: Brook Acre Primary School recently marked World Book Day with a vibrant celebration centred around an orange theme, bringing the joy of reading and storytelling to life for its pupils. The school's creative approach to the annual literary celebration drew inspiration from There's a Rang-tan in My Bedroom, a children's book that has captured the imagination of young readers across the country. By adopting the distinctive orange colour associated with the story, the school created an immersive experience that encouraged children to engage with literature in a fun and memorable way. World Book Day is an important occasion in the school calendar, dedicated to fostering a love of reading and celebrating the power of books and authors. Brook Acre Primary School's decision to theme their event around a specific children's title demonstrates how schools can make the day more engaging and interactive for their students. The celebration highlighted the school's commitment to promoting literacy and storytelling among its pupils. By connecting the day's activities to a popular children's book, the school helped young readers discover new stories and understand the magic that books can bring into their lives. The orange theme served as a visual anchor for the day's events, making the celebration instantly recognisable and exciting for the children. Such initiatives play a vital role in developing children's reading habits from an early age. When schools create special occasions around books and authors, they reinforce the message that reading is valued and celebrated within the school community. This approach can inspire children to explore more stories and develop a lifelong passion for literature. Brook Acre Primary School's World Book Day celebration is a testament to the creative ways schools across the region are encouraging young people to embrace reading and storytelling. The event brought together pupils, staff, and families in a shared appreciation of children's literature and the imaginative worlds that books can open up.
summary: Brook Acre Primary School celebrated World Book Day with an orange theme, inspired by There’s a Rang-tan in My Bedroom, promoting reading and storytelling.

title: Indonesia to ban 'high risk' social media for under-16s
content: Indonesia has announced plans to ban access to high-risk social media platforms for children under 16, marking a significant move by the world's fourth most populous nation to protect young users online. The decision targets platforms deemed particularly dangerous due to their potential to expose minors to harmful content, cyberbullying, or addictive behaviours. Officials have highlighted concerns over the mental health impacts on Indonesia's youth, where social media usage has surged in recent years amid widespread smartphone adoption. This policy positions Indonesia alongside a growing list of countries tightening digital restrictions for minors. Australia recently introduced similar age limits on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, while the UK and parts of Europe are debating comparable measures. In Indonesia, with over 270 million people and a massive young population, the ban aims to curb what authorities describe as an epidemic of online risks. The government plans to enforce the restrictions through age verification systems and app store controls, though details on implementation remain under discussion. Critics worry about enforcement challenges in a country with vast rural areas and limited digital literacy, but supporters argue it sends a strong message on safeguarding childhood. Indonesia's Communications Minister emphasised that the focus is on high-risk sites, sparing educational or low-harm platforms. This follows years of public campaigns against online predation and excessive screen time, with studies showing links to rising anxiety and sleep disorders among teens. Parents and educators have welcomed the step, calling it overdue in a nation where children as young as 10 often have unrestricted access. Schools may play a role in awareness drives, while tech firms face pressure to comply or risk fines. The announcement underscores a global shift towards parental controls and age-appropriate digital spaces. As Indonesia rolls out the policy, it could influence other Southeast Asian nations grappling with similar issues, prompting debates on balancing freedom of expression with child welfare. Experts predict initial resistance from users and platforms, but long-term benefits for mental wellbeing. For now, families are urged to monitor usage and explore safer alternatives, as the country leads by example in the fight against digital dangers.
summary: Indonesia has become the latest and most populous country to say it will ban social media for under-16s.
author: Sky News

title: Remembering the old Warrington Odeon cinema and the stories it brings back
content: Warrington's iconic old Odeon cinema has stirred a wave of nostalgia among locals, with residents flooding social media with heartfelt stories of bygone eras. The once-thriving picture house, a staple of the town's cultural life, continues to evoke powerful memories decades after its heyday. Social media platforms have lit up with posts from Warrington folk reminiscing about their first dates under the cinema's glowing marquee. Couples recall the flutter of excitement as they shared popcorn and watched romances unfold on the big screen, the dim lights and velvet seats creating the perfect backdrop for young love. Classic films top the list of treasured recollections. From epic blockbusters to timeless British favourites, moviegoers describe the thrill of queuing for hours to catch the latest releases. One common thread is the sense of community, where families and friends gathered weekly, escaping everyday worries into worlds of adventure and drama. Childhood memories dominate many accounts, painting vivid pictures of Saturday morning matinees. Kids speak fondly of rushing home from school, pockets full of pocket money for sweets and tickets. The Odeon's grand interior, with its ornate decorations and booming sound, left an indelible mark on young imaginations, fostering a lifelong passion for cinema. These stories highlight how the Odeon was more than just a building; it was a social hub that shaped Warrington's identity. Demolition or redevelopment may have claimed the physical structure, but its spirit endures through these shared experiences. Locals express a mix of sadness for what's lost and gratitude for the joy it brought. The surge in online reminiscing, sparked by recent posts and throwback photos, has connected generations. Younger residents discover their parents' tales, while elders relive glory days. It's a reminder of Warrington's rich entertainment history, urging the community to preserve such landmarks in collective memory. As digital archives grow, the old Odeon stands as a symbol of simpler times. Whether it was sneaking in extra friends or cheering at cliffhangers, these anecdotes capture the magic that made cinema-going an unforgettable ritual in Warrington life. The conversations show no sign of slowing, keeping the cinema's legacy flickering brightly.
summary: Warrington’s old Odeon cinema sparks nostalgia as locals share cherished memories of first dates, classic films, and childhood moments on social media.
author: Warrington Guardian

title: Green belt garden centre site proposed to become holiday chalet park
content: A garden centre and nursery site nestled in Warrington's green belt could soon undergo a dramatic transformation into a holiday chalet park, sparking interest among locals and planners alike. The proposal, centred on White Moss Nursery and Garden Centre, aims to repurpose the existing site to accommodate a cluster of holiday chalets. This move reflects a growing trend in rural areas where traditional agricultural or retail operations evolve to meet demands for short-term leisure stays. Green belt land, designated to prevent urban sprawl and preserve countryside character, rarely sees such developments. Proponents argue the change could breathe new life into a site no longer viable as a nursery, offering tourism boosts without expanding built-up areas significantly. Local residents have mixed views. Some welcome the potential for jobs in hospitality and maintenance, alongside visitor spending at nearby businesses. Others worry about increased traffic on rural lanes and the erosion of green belt protections, even if the footprint remains similar to the current structures. Warrington Borough Council will scrutinise the plans, weighing environmental impacts, flood risks in the mossy terrain, and alignment with national planning policies. Chalets, typically low-rise and timber-framed, might blend into the landscape more seamlessly than sprawling retail sheds, but biodiversity assessments will be key. This isn't the first time green belt sites have faced repurposing bids. Similar schemes elsewhere have succeeded by demonstrating "very special circumstances," like economic viability or lack of alternative sites. Here, the garden centre's operators highlight shifting consumer habits, with online plant sales and garden supplies diminishing footfall. If approved, the chalet park could draw families seeking peaceful escapes close to the M62 corridor, with walks amid mosslands and proximity to Cheshire's beauty spots. Construction might start next year, pending consents, creating seasonal employment. Campaigners for green belt integrity urge caution, calling for robust public consultation. The planning application, lodged recently, invites feedback from the community, underscoring the delicate balance between development and conservation in Warrington's fringes. As deliberations progress, the fate of White Moss hangs in the balance, emblematic of broader tensions in Britain's planning landscape where leisure tourism vies with land safeguards.
summary: A GARDEN centre and nursery site in the green belt is proposed to be transformed to become a holiday chalet park.
author: Warrington Guardian

title: Anthropic labelled a supply chain risk by Pentagon
content: The Pentagon has officially designated leading AI firm Anthropic as a supply chain risk, marking the first time a US company has received such a label typically reserved for foreign adversaries. This unprecedented move stems from a heated dispute between the Department of Defense and Anthropic over restrictions the company imposed on its Claude AI model. Anthropic has refused to allow the military to use the technology for certain applications, including mass surveillance of American citizens or powering fully autonomous weapons without human oversight in targeting or firing decisions. Pentagon officials argue that no private vendor should dictate limits on the lawful use of vital capabilities by the armed forces, potentially undermining service members' safety and operational needs. The designation, formally notified to Anthropic's leadership on March 4, requires companies and agencies working with the Pentagon to certify they do not use Anthropic's models in those contracts. This could force government contractors to sever ties with the firm for federal work, disrupting partnerships across the defence sector. While the label does not extend to purely commercial uses, broader statements from officials suggest defence contractors should avoid any dealings with Anthropic, pending clarification on the exact legal scope. The conflict escalated after Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei informed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that the company would not lift its safeguards. President Trump had previously directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic's AI, prompting threats to invoke authorities like the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act. Critics, including former Trump adviser Dean Ball, have decried the action as overly aggressive, likening it to treating domestic innovators worse than foreign rivals and calling it a troubling shift in government strategy. Anthropic has vowed to challenge the designation in court, asserting it is legally unsound and narrowly scoped under relevant statutes like 10 USC 3252, which mandates the least restrictive means to protect supply chains. The company emphasised that most customers remain unaffected and pledged to continue providing Claude to the military at nominal cost during any transition, prioritising national security needs amid ongoing operations, such as those in the Middle East where the AI supports data management. Tech industry voices, including employees from rivals like OpenAI and Google, have rallied against the move, urging Congress to intervene and defending firms' rights to set ethical boundaries on their technology. As litigation looms, the saga highlights deepening tensions between rapid AI advancement and military demands, with potential ripple effects for the entire US tech ecosystem and federal procurement.
summary: The supply chain risk designation of the artificial intelligence firm is a first for a US company.
author: BBC News

title: States sue Trump administration over new 'unlawful' global tariffs
content: A coalition of 24 US states has launched a high-stakes legal challenge against the Trump administration's latest push for sweeping global tariffs. Led by Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, the group includes attorneys general from states such as Arizona, California, and New York. They argue the new tariffs are unlawful and represent an overreach of presidential power without congressional approval. The lawsuit, filed in the US Court of International Trade, seeks an immediate injunction to halt the policy before it causes widespread economic disruption. State officials held a press conference to spotlight their case, describing the tariffs as the largest tax increase on Americans without legislative backing. They contend the administration is misusing Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a provision never invoked by any previous president. This legal battle follows closely on the heels of a Supreme Court ruling that struck down an earlier set of Trump tariffs. Hours after that decision, the administration announced these replacements, imposing levies reported between 10% and 15% on most products from around the world. Critics among the states highlight that the law was designed for rare currency crises, which they say do not exist today. They also accuse the policy of uneven application, with certain industries receiving exemptions. The move underscores deepening tensions over trade authority in the US. Proponents of the tariffs view them as essential tools to protect domestic industries and address global trade imbalances. However, opponents warn of higher costs for consumers, supply chain disruptions, and retaliatory measures from trading partners. Oregon's leadership in the suit reflects its heavy reliance on international trade, particularly in agriculture and technology sectors vulnerable to such levies. As the case unfolds, businesses and economists are watching closely. The court could set a precedent on the limits of executive power in trade matters. State leaders expressed hope for a swift ruling, echoing their frustration with what they call creative legal manoeuvres to bypass Congress. This challenge arrives amid broader debates on economic policy, with implications for jobs, prices, and international relations. The administration has yet to respond formally to the lawsuit, but past defences have emphasised national security and economic sovereignty. For now, the states' bid to block the tariffs keeps the spotlight on a contentious front in America's trade wars.
summary: The 24 states are seeking to block Trump's latest tariffs, which he imposed to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court.
author: BBC News
